prime.problem: After fixing divergence and bank conflicts, the reduction still uses only 11% of the G80's bandwidth. Half the threads never add anything, most tree steps are nearly empty, and the loop's bookkeeping costs more than the adds. Unless the algorithm changes shape, polishing the code only makes an idle tree cheaper.
prime.fits: Part II of Harris's reduction. Part I fixed which thread adds which pair; this card changes how much each thread does. It reuses occupancy's lesson (more independent work per thread hides latency) and the first kernel's grid-stride loop, and ends with the modern warp-shuffle rewrite.
prime.goal: Explain why cascading beats unrolling, compute Brent's cost for a given thread count, and write the last warp of a reduction safely on Volta and later.

attend: At 17 GB/s kernel 4 is far below the 86.4 GB/s peak, yet the slides call it instruction-bound. What evidence supports that, and what does it rule out?
Why does unrolling the last warp save work in every warp, not only the last one?
What does "cost = processors × time" count that plain time doesn't, and why does P = N make the tree cost-inefficient?
In kernel 7, how does i += gridSize keep a warp's loads coalesced while each thread sums hundreds of elements?
Why is the slides' volatile warp reduction unsafe on a T4 or H100, and what replaces it?

must: Tree over N with one thread per element → log2 N steps but cost N·log2 N (22 N for 2^22) → Brent: use ~N/log2 N threads, each summing ~log2 N elements first → cost falls toward 2N → same sum, about 11× less machine time

Each thread first sums many elements serially (cascading) → the tree becomes a short tail on a mostly busy kernel → more independent loads per thread hide latency (Volkov) and fewer blocks shrink the recursive launches → kernel 7 reaches 72.5% of peak

Once memory is not saturated and intensity is tiny, the bottleneck is instructions (address math, loop counters, barriers) → unrolling removes them (1.8 × 1.41 = 2.54×) → but it only makes an idle tree cheaper, which is why the algorithmic changes gave 11.84× and should come first

Since Volta, warp lanes are not guaranteed to run in lock-step → lanes communicating through shared memory without sync can read stale values → use __shfl_down_sync (register exchange) or put __syncwarp() between every read and write
elevated: Block size as a template parameter → every if (blockSize >= …) is resolved at compile time → the unrolled tree has no runtime branches → libraries still template on block size for the same reason
reference: the kernel-by-kernel times and GB/s (0.965, 0.536, 0.381, 0.268 ms)
the switch over 10 block sizes that picks a template instantiation
the slides' best G80 configuration (64–256 blocks of 128 threads)
source quirks: reduce5/reduce6 naming, warpReduce without the template argument, the 512-thread G80 limit

compress.prompt: From memory, write the reduction ladder as two columns, "algorithmic" and "code", with each kernel's change in one line and the product of each column. Then add one line on why the algorithmic column should be done first.
checklist: algorithmic: addressing (kernels 2, 3), first add during load (4), cascading (7): 11.84×
code: unroll last warp (5), full template unroll (6): 2.54×
algorithm decides how much work and idleness there is; unrolling only cheapens each step
Brent: O(N / log N) threads doing O(log N) serial adds keeps cost O(N)
on Volta+, the last warp uses shuffles or __syncwarp, not volatile

retrieve.q: Explain why Brent's theorem says to use fewer threads than elements, when fewer threads means each one takes longer.
answer: with P = N the tree has most processors idle in most steps, so machine time (cost) is N·log N
fewer threads doing serial adds first keep every processor busy
total time barely grows (22 → 44 steps in the model) but cost drops from 22 N to 2 N

retrieve.q: Walk through kernel 7 for one block: what each thread does in the while loop, why the loop stride is blockSize·2·gridDim.x, and what happens after it.
answer: each thread adds g_idata[i] + g_idata[i + blockSize] into a register-backed partial sum, then jumps a whole grid ahead
the stride keeps neighbouring threads on neighbouring addresses every iteration, so loads stay coalesced
then one barrier and kernel 6's unrolled tree, ending in the warp reduction
at 2^22 ints and 64 blocks, 512 serial adds per thread before a 7-step tree

retrieve.q: Your RMSNorm kernel reduces 4,096 values per token. Compare 4,096 threads with a pure tree against 128 threads that each sum 32 values first: work, steps and Brent cost.
answer: 128 threads: 31 serial adds + 7 tree steps = 38 steps, cost 128 × 38 = 4,864 ≈ 1.19 N
the cascaded version is ~10× cheaper in machine time and uses one block, but its latency is longer in steps; on a GPU the idle threads in the first version would be wasted slots other rows could use

compare.q: Kernel 7 and Volkov's matmul both win by giving each thread more work. What does "more work per thread" hide or save in each case, and what limits how far you can push it?
answer: reduction: many independent loads in flight per thread hide DRAM latency, and fewer blocks cut launch levels
matmul: register reuse cuts shared-memory reads per FMA
limits: reduction needs enough threads to cover ~100 KB in flight and every SM busy; matmul runs out of registers (255 per thread) and occupancy

compare.q: Harris uses kernel launches as the global sync; the fusion card treats launches as overhead to remove. When is a multi-launch reduction the right design, and when would you fuse the reduction into a neighbouring kernel instead?
answer: multi-launch fits one huge array: the launch is the only grid-wide barrier, and cascading keeps the number of levels small
fusion fits many small rows (RMSNorm, softmax): each row fits in one block, so no global sync is needed
on an H100 a 16.8 MB sum takes ~5 µs of DRAM time, so a few µs per launch is a large share

predict.q: You rewrite kernel 5's last warp with __shfl_down_sync but skip cascading (each thread still adds just two elements). Commit: on a modern GPU, do you expect a speed-up near kernel 7's, near kernel 5's, or somewhere else, and why?
predict.answer: Near kernel 5's, not kernel 7's. Shuffles make the last 5 steps correct and a little cheaper (registers instead of shared memory), but they touch only the tail of each block. The dominant waste, a mostly idle tree after only two elements per thread and many blocks and launches, is untouched. Only cascading (kernel 7's grid-stride loop) removes that, which is why the slides' algorithmic column (11.84×) dwarfs the code column (2.54×).
